claims.text: A neural-network interatomic potential trained on ab initio solid and high-temperature liquid configurations will more accurately represent the configurational diversity of multicomponent HEAs near melting.
The proposed potential will improve reference–target phase-space overlap with the ab initio system.
The proposed potential will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD EAM references.
Nearly equiatomic NbTaTiV is a representative refractory or transition-metal high-entropy alloy for this intervention.
Training must include both high-temperature liquid snapshots and corresponding solid configurations.
The intervention is applicable to nearly equiatomic HEAs at or near their melting points and across the solid–liquid transition.
Neural-network potentials can represent a vast variety of atomic configurations and many-body interactions.
Greater representation of configurations and many-body interactions yields a higher-fidelity potential-energy surface.
Including high-temperature ab initio liquid data enables the potential to capture subtle liquid configurational variations.
Traditional EAM potentials miss subtle configurational variations and many-body interactions relevant to the ab initio liquid.
A closer match between the machine-learned reference and the ab initio target reduces mismatch along the thermodynamic-integration path.
The intervention may reduce integration-path mismatch by approximately 30–50%.
The intervention will improve free-energy calculation accuracy relative to TOR-TILD EAM references.
TOR-TILD's standard EAM references have limited configurational representation and produce significant path mismatch and free-energy errors, especially for ab initio liquids.
Effectiveness for strongly compositionally asymmetric alloys or temperatures far from melting is untested.
Training-data quality and transferability between HEA systems may affect the improvement obtained.
Failure to achieve a statistically significant improvement, exemplified as less than a 20–30% reduction in path mismatch, or failure to improve phase-space overlap would falsify the hypothesis.
